claim: Deletion of the PEX1 gene promotes pexophagy under nitrogen starvation.
source: We confirmed that deletion of the PEX1 gene encoding a subunit of the exportomer promotes pexophagy under nitrogen starvation (Nuttall et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and is consistent with prior citation (Nuttall et al., 2014).

claim: Pexophagy induced by PEX1 deletion is dependent on the pexophagy receptor Atg36.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed that this process is dependent on the pexophagy receptor Atg36 as well as Atg11, a scaffold protein that connects autophagy receptors to the Atg1 complex involved in all forms of autophagy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pexophagy induced by PEX1 deletion is dependent on Atg11.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed that this process is dependent on the pexophagy receptor Atg36 as well as Atg11, a scaffold protein that connects autophagy receptors to the Atg1 complex involved in all forms of autophagy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Atg11 is a scaffold protein that connects autophagy receptors to the Atg1 complex involved in all forms of autophagy.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed that this process is dependent on the pexophagy receptor Atg36 as well as Atg11, a scaffold protein that connects autophagy receptors to the Atg1 complex involved in all forms of autophagy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Atg11's function.

claim: Pexophagy induced by PEX1 deletion is associated with a modified form of Atg36 that can be resolved by SDS-PAGE.
source: and is associated with a modified form of Atg36 that could be resolved by sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE; Nuttall et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and is consistent with prior citation (Nuttall et al., 2014).

claim: Exportomer mutations enhance removal of peroxisomes but not mitochondria or bulk cytoplasm.
source: Exportomer mutations have been previously shown to enhance removal of peroxisomes but not mitochondria or bulk cytoplasm, thus allowing the autophagy system to effectively exert a form of organelle quality control (Nuttall et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Nuttall et al., 2014).

claim: Atg36 is activated by Hrr25-mediated phosphorylation during nitrogen starvation.
source: In this latter, nonselective context, Atg36 is activated by Hrr25-mediated phosphorylation resulting in the enhanced ability of the modified receptor product to interact with Atg11 (Tanaka et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Tanaka et al., 2014).

claim: Hrr25-mediated phosphorylation of Atg36 results in enhanced ability of Atg36 to interact with Atg11.
source: In this latter, nonselective context, Atg36 is activated by Hrr25-mediated phosphorylation resulting in the enhanced ability of the modified receptor product to interact with Atg11 (Tanaka et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Tanaka et al., 2014).

claim: Lambda phosphatase treatment converts modified Atg36 from pex1∆ cells to its unmodified form.
source: First, lambda phosphatase treatment of Atg36-MYC isolated by affinity purification from a pex1∆ cell extract converted modified Atg36 to its unmodified form, thus rendering its migration indistinguishable from the wild-type control (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Atg36 is not modified in the presence of a Pex3 mutation (pex3-177) that abolishes Atg36 phosphorylation by Hrr25 during nitrogen starvation.
source: Second, Atg36 was no longer modified in the presence of a Pex3 mutation (pex3-177) (Figure 1B) that abolishes Atg36 phosphorylation by Hrr25 during nitrogen starvation (Meguro et al., 2020; Motley et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and is consistent with prior citations (Meguro et al., 2020; Motley et al., 2012).

claim: The pex3-177 mutation abolishes Atg36 phosphorylation by Hrr25 during nitrogen starvation.
source: Second, Atg36 was no longer modified in the presence of a Pex3 mutation (pex3-177) (Figure 1B) that abolishes Atg36 phosphorylation by Hrr25 during nitrogen starvation (Meguro et al., 2020; Motley et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Meguro et al., 2020; Motley et al., 2012).

claim: Auxin-inducible degradation (AID) of Pex1 enhances pexophagy.
source: Third, we took advantage of the previous observation that auxin-inducible degradation (AID) of Pex1 can also enhance pexophagy (Nuttall et al., 2014; Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and is consistent with prior citation (Nuttall et al., 2014).

claim: Simultaneous AID of Hrr25 suppresses the pexophagy phenotype caused by conditional pex1 degradation.
source: We were then able to effectively suppress this conditional pex1 phenotype by simultaneous AID of Hrr25 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pexophagy enhanced by the loss of Pex1 is abolished by inhibiting the kinase activity of a Shokat mutant version of Hrr25 with the ATP analog 1NM-PP1.
source: Lastly, we found that pexophagy enhanced by the loss of Pex1 was abolished by inhibiting the kinase activity of a Shokat mutant version of Hrr25 with the ATP analog 1NM-PP1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Exportomer mutants enable Atg36 phosphoactivation by Hrr25, leading to selective pexophagy in the absence of nutritional stress.
source: In sum, these data show that exportomer mutants enable Atg36 phosphoactivation by Hrr25, thus leading to selective pexophagy in the absence of nutritional stress.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: The exportomer enables the recycling of several receptors for targeting and translocation of matrix proteins with peroxisome targeting signals (PTSs).
source: The exportomer enables the recycling of several receptors for targeting and translocation of matrix proteins with peroxisome targeting signals (PTSs).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the exportomer's function.

claim: The mechanoenzymatic process of PTS receptor recycling appears to be driven by the Pex1/6 ATPase.
source: This mechanoenzymatic process has not been fully reconstituted with purified components but appears to be driven by the Pex1/6 ATPase.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from existing knowledge about the exportomer.

claim: Mutation of the D2 Walker B motif of Pex6 (E832A) abrogates ATP hydrolysis by the Pex1/6 complex in vitro.
source: To test if the latter activity also drives Atg36 repression, we mutated the D2 Walker B motif of Pex6, mutation of which was recently shown to abrogate ATP hydrolysis by the Pex1/6 complex in vitro , without affecting hexamerization of Pex6 with wild-type Pex1 subunits (Ciniawsky et al., 2015) or Pex6 binding to Pex15 (Birschmann et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Ciniawsky et al., 2015).

claim: The D2 Walker B motif mutation of Pex6 (E832A) does not affect hexamerization of Pex6 with wild-type Pex1 subunits.
source: To test if the latter activity also drives Atg36 repression, we mutated the D2 Walker B motif of Pex6, mutation of which was recently shown to abrogate ATP hydrolysis by the Pex1/6 complex in vitro , without affecting hexamerization of Pex6 with wild-type Pex1 subunits (Ciniawsky et al., 2015) or Pex6 binding to Pex15 (Birschmann et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Ciniawsky et al., 2015).

claim: The D2 Walker B motif mutation of Pex6 (E832A) does not affect Pex6 binding to Pex15.
source: To test if the latter activity also drives Atg36 repression, we mutated the D2 Walker B motif of Pex6, mutation of which was recently shown to abrogate ATP hydrolysis by the Pex1/6 complex in vitro , without affecting hexamerization of Pex6 with wild-type Pex1 subunits (Ciniawsky et al., 2015) or Pex6 binding to Pex15 (Birschmann et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Birschmann et al., 2003).

claim: In cells expressing Pex6WB (E832A), Atg36 phosphoactivation and pexophagy are induced to a similar degree as in pex6∆ cells.
source: In cells expressing this point mutant version of Pex6 (E832A, Pex6WB), Atg36 phosphoactivation and pexophagy were induced to a similar degree as in pex6∆ cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Exportomer ATPase activity, either directly or indirectly, inhibits Atg36.
source: These findings demonstrate that exportomer ATPase activity, either directly or indirectly, inhibits Atg36.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that the ATPase-defective mutant induces Atg36 phosphorylation.

claim: PTS receptors have been excluded as potential mediators of Atg36 activation in pex1∆ cells.
source: PTS receptors have already been excluded as potential mediators of Atg36 activation in pex1∆ cells (Nuttall et al., 2014), but a systematic dissection of this mechanism in vivo had not been carried out.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Nuttall et al., 2014).

claim: Atg36 has relatively low cell abundance.
source: Atg36 has relatively low cell abundance and appears to be both inherently unstable and resistant to Hrr25 phosphorylation when not associated with Pex3, its peroxisomal anchor (Meguro et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an observation about Atg36 properties.

claim: Atg36 appears to be inherently unstable when not associated with Pex3.
source: Atg36 has relatively low cell abundance and appears to be both inherently unstable and resistant to Hrr25 phosphorylation when not associated with Pex3, its peroxisomal anchor (Meguro et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Meguro et al., 2020).

claim: Atg36 is resistant to Hrr25 phosphorylation when not associated with Pex3.
source: Atg36 has relatively low cell abundance and appears to be both inherently unstable and resistant to Hrr25 phosphorylation when not associated with Pex3, its peroxisomal anchor (Meguro et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Meguro et al., 2020).

claim: Pex3 is the peroxisomal anchor for Atg36.
source: Atg36 has relatively low cell abundance and appears to be both inherently unstable and resistant to Hrr25 phosphorylation when not associated with Pex3, its peroxisomal anchor (Meguro et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Meguro et al., 2020).

claim: Comparative mass spectrometry of Pex3-FLAG affinity purification revealed the presence of several previously identified Pex3 interaction partners, including Atg36, Inp1, Pex19, and Pex5.
source: Comparative mass spectrometry with extracts of control cells expressing untagged Pex3 revealed the presence of several previously identified Pex3 interaction partners, including Atg36, Inp1, Pex19, and Pex5, as well as several peroxisome membrane proteins whose insertion is known to be Pex19- and Pex3 dependent (Fang et al., 2004; Hettema et al., 2000; Jones et al., 2001; Sacksteder et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mass spectrometry data and citations to prior work (Fang et al., 2004; Hettema et al., 2000; Jones et al., 2001; Sacksteder et al., 2000).

claim: Comparative mass spectrometry of Pex3-FLAG affinity purification revealed several peroxisome membrane proteins whose insertion is known to be Pex19- and Pex3 dependent.
source: Comparative mass spectrometry with extracts of control cells expressing untagged Pex3 revealed the presence of several previously identified Pex3 interaction partners, including Atg36, Inp1, Pex19, and Pex5, as well as several peroxisome membrane proteins whose insertion is known to be Pex19- and Pex3 dependent (Fang et al., 2004; Hettema et al., 2000; Jones et al., 2001; Sacksteder et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mass spectrometry data and citations to prior work (Fang et al., 2004; Hettema et al., 2000; Jones et al., 2001; Sacksteder et al., 2000).

claim: All three components of the exportomer (Pex1, Pex6, Pex15) were identified in Pex3-FLAG affinity purification by mass spectrometry.
source: Intriguingly, we also identified all three components of the exportomer, which to our knowledge had not been previously linked to Pex3.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mass spectrometry data.

claim: The exportomer components had not been previously linked to Pex3.
source: Intriguingly, we also identified all three components of the exportomer, which to our knowledge had not been previously linked to Pex3.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Pex1 is a relatively abundant component of the Pex3 interactome.
source: Indeed, we confirmed that Pex1 was a relatively abundant component of the Pex3 interactome by appending a bulky tag (3xV5-AID; ~30 kDa) to its C-terminus and detecting it by western blotting, as well as by the expected band shift following SDS–PAGE analysis (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The coimmunoprecipitation between Pex3 and Pex1 is not affected by the expression of Pex6WB.
source: We found that the coimmunoprecipitation between Pex3 and Pex1 was not affected by the expression of Pex6WB (Figure 2C), suggesting that the effect of this mutation on Atg36 phosphorylation and pexophagy induction (Figure 1D) is not simply caused by gross disruption of Pex3's association with the exportomer.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The effect of the Pex6WB mutation on Atg36 phosphorylation and pexophagy induction is not simply caused by gross disruption of Pex3's association with the exportomer.
source: We found that the coimmunoprecipitation between Pex3 and Pex1 was not affected by the expression of Pex6WB (Figure 2C), suggesting that the effect of this mutation on Atg36 phosphorylation and pexophagy induction (Figure 1D) is not simply caused by gross disruption of Pex3's association with the exportomer.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that Pex3-Pex1 interaction is maintained in the Pex6WB mutant.

claim: Quantitative mass spectrometry analysis of immunopurified Pex3 from pex1∆ cells revealed an 11-fold depletion of Pex6.
source: Quantitative mass spectrometry analysis of immunopurified Pex3 from pex1∆ cells revealed the expected depletion of Pex6 (11-fold) and a lesser depletion of Pex15 (1.9-fold) (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Quantitative mass spectrometry analysis of immunopurified Pex3 from pex1∆ cells revealed a 1.9-fold depletion of Pex15.
source: Quantitative mass spectrometry analysis of immunopurified Pex3 from pex1∆ cells revealed the expected depletion of Pex6 (11-fold) and a lesser depletion of Pex15 (1.9-fold) (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Quantitative mass spectrometry analysis of immunopurified Pex3 from pex1∆ cells revealed no significant depletion or enrichment of Pex5, Pex19, or known Pex19 clients.
source: By contrast, we observed no significant depletion or enrichment of Pex5, Pex19, or known Pex19 clients, suggesting that Pex1 loss does not alter the interaction between Pex3 and any of its other known binding partners detectable by this method (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Pex1 loss does not alter the interaction between Pex3 and any of its other known binding partners detectable by mass spectrometry.
source: By contrast, we observed no significant depletion or enrichment of Pex5, Pex19, or known Pex19 clients, suggesting that Pex1 loss does not alter the interaction between Pex3 and any of its other known binding partners detectable by this method (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mass spectrometry data showing no changes in other Pex3 interactors.

claim: The quantitative interactome analysis revealed a direct physical link between the exportomer and Atg36 bound to Pex3.
source: In sum, our quantitative interactome analysis revealed a direct physical link between the exportomer and Atg36 bound to Pex3 but found no evidence of exportomer-dependent interactions that mediate Atg36 activation by Hrr25.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined mass spectrometry data.

claim: The quantitative interactome analysis found no evidence of exportomer-dependent interactions that mediate Atg36 activation by Hrr25.
source: In sum, our quantitative interactome analysis revealed a direct physical link between the exportomer and Atg36 bound to Pex3 but found no evidence of exportomer-dependent interactions that mediate Atg36 activation by Hrr25.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined mass spectrometry data.

claim: The absence of Pex19 is sufficient to induce Atg36 phosphorylation comparably to exportomer pex mutations.
source: However, we found that the absence of Pex19 was actually by itself sufficient to induce Atg36 phosphorylation comparably to exportomer pex mutations (Figure 3A and Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 1B.

claim: Analysis of Pex3 immunopurified from pex19∆ cells revealed that the Pex3-Pex1 interaction was lost in pex19∆ cells.
source: Analysis of Pex3 immunopurified from pex19∆ cells revealed that the Pex3-Pex1 interaction was lost in pex19∆ cells, suggesting that the effect of Pex19 on Atg36 phosphorylation was indirectly caused by disruption of the exportomer's proximity to Atg36 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The effect of Pex19 on Atg36 phosphorylation is indirectly caused by disruption of the exportomer's proximity to Atg36.
source: Analysis of Pex3 immunopurified from pex19∆ cells revealed that the Pex3-Pex1 interaction was lost in pex19∆ cells, suggesting that the effect of Pex19 on Atg36 phosphorylation was indirectly caused by disruption of the exportomer's proximity to Atg36 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing loss of Pex3-Pex1 interaction in pex19∆ cells.

claim: Expressing a cytosolic form of Pex3 promotes Atg36 phosphorylation.
source: A previous study focused on pexophagy regulation by nutritional stress showed that expressing a cytosolic form of Pex3 promotes Atg36 phosphorylation (Meguro et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Meguro et al., 2020).

claim: The cytoPex3 mutant enables Atg36 phosphorylation in the cytosol of postlogarithmic cells.
source: Similarly, we found that our cytoPex3 mutant also enabled Atg36 phosphorylation in the cytosol of postlogarithmic cells (Figure 3C) but was defective in Pex11-GFP processing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The cytoPex3 mutant is defective in Pex11-GFP processing.
source: Similarly, we found that our cytoPex3 mutant also enabled Atg36 phosphorylation in the cytosol of postlogarithmic cells (Figure 3C) but was defective in Pex11-GFP processing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In cells expressing cytoPex15–cytoPex3, Atg36 phosphorylation is repressed compared to cells expressing cytoPex3.
source: Strikingly, in cells expressing cytoPex15–cytoPex3, compared to cells expressing cytoPex3, we observed repression of Atg36 phosphorylation, but not when we caused AID of Pex1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Repression of Atg36 phosphorylation by cytoPex15–cytoPex3 is lost when Pex1 is degraded by AID.
source: Strikingly, in cells expressing cytoPex15–cytoPex3, compared to cells expressing cytoPex3, we observed repression of Atg36 phosphorylation, but not when we caused AID of Pex1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the cytoPex15–cytoPex3 engineered context, repression of Atg36 phosphorylation is no longer dependent on Pex19.
source: Importantly, in this engineered context, repression was no longer dependent on Pex19 but remained driven by the exportomer's ATPase activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: In the cytoPex15–cytoPex3 engineered context, repression of Atg36 phosphorylation remains driven by the exportomer's ATPase activity.
source: Importantly, in this engineered context, repression was no longer dependent on Pex19 but remained driven by the exportomer's ATPase activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The exportomer's proximity to Atg36 is critical for inhibition of pexophagy.
source: These data demonstrate that the exportomer's proximity to Atg36 is critical for inhibition of pexophagy but that Pex19 and peroxisomal membrane proteins are not strictly required for repression of Atg36 phosphorylation by Pex1/6.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data with the cytoPex15–cytoPex3 system.

claim: Pex19 and peroxisomal membrane proteins are not strictly required for repression of Atg36 phosphorylation by Pex1/6.
source: These data demonstrate that the exportomer's proximity to Atg36 is critical for inhibition of pexophagy but that Pex19 and peroxisomal membrane proteins are not strictly required for repression of Atg36 phosphorylation by Pex1/6.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data with the cytoPex15–cytoPex3 system.

claim: Quantitative proteomics analysis revealed that the amounts of Pex1 and Pex6 present in the cytoPex15–cytoPex3 complex are not affected by the pex6WB mutation.
source: Quantitative proteomics analysis revealed that the amounts of Pex1 and Pex6 present in the cytoPex15–cytoPex3 complex were not affected, nor was the amount of Inp1, a soluble protein involved in peroxisome inheritance, which, like Atg36, binds Pex3 (Figure 3D; Fagarasanu et al., 2005, Munck et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The amount of Inp1 in the cytoPex15–cytoPex3 complex is not affected by the pex6WB mutation.
source: Quantitative proteomics analysis revealed that the amounts of Pex1 and Pex6 present in the cytoPex15–cytoPex3 complex were not affected, nor was the amount of Inp1, a soluble protein involved in peroxisome inheritance, which, like Atg36, binds Pex3 (Figure 3D; Fagarasanu et al., 2005, Munck et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Inp1 is a soluble protein involved in peroxisome inheritance that binds Pex3.
source: Quantitative proteomics analysis revealed that the amounts of Pex1 and Pex6 present in the cytoPex15–cytoPex3 complex were not affected, nor was the amount of Inp1, a soluble protein involved in peroxisome inheritance, which, like Atg36, binds Pex3 (Figure 3D; Fagarasanu et al., 2005, Munck et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Fagarasanu et al., 2005, Munck et al., 2009).

claim: The abundance of Atg36 is increased ~2.2-fold in cytoPex15–cytoPex3 complexes isolated from cells expressing Pex6WB.
source: Notably, the abundance of Atg36 was increased ~2.2-fold in cytoPex15–cytoPex3 complexes isolated from cells expressing Pex6WB (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The interactome analysis supports the model that the exportomer directly blocks activation of Pex3-bound Atg36 by Hrr25.
source: In sum, our interactome analysis supports the model that the exportomer directly blocks activation of Pex3-bound Atg36 by Hrr25.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined mass spectrometry data.

claim: Pex15's soluble domain can dynamically control the ATPase activity of Pex1/6.
source: A previous study focused on the exportomer's role in PTS receptor recycling noted the ability of Pex15's soluble domain to dynamically control the ATPase activity of Pex1/6 (Gardner et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Gardner et al., 2018).

claim: In cells coexpressing Pex3-FRB and FKBP-Pex6, addition of rapamycin represses Atg36 phosphorylation.
source: In cells coexpressing Pex3-FRB and FKBP-Pex6, but not cells expressing Pex3-FRB and FKBP-Pex6WB, addition of rapamycin repressed Atg36 phosphorylation (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In cells expressing Pex3-FRB and FKBP-Pex6WB, addition of rapamycin does not repress Atg36 phosphorylation.
source: In cells coexpressing Pex3-FRB and FKBP-Pex6, but not cells expressing Pex3-FRB and FKBP-Pex6WB, addition of rapamycin repressed Atg36 phosphorylation (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: When Cdc48 is recruited to Pex3 through the FRB/Rap/FKBP system, Atg36 phosphorylation is not repressed under rapamycin treatment.
source: When a AAA ATPase involved in ER-associated degradation, Cdc48, was recruited to Pex3 through the similar FRB/Rap/FKBP system (cells coexpressing Pex3-FRB and FKBP-Cdc48), Atg36 phosphorylation was not repressed under rapamycin treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Cdc48 is a AAA ATPase involved in ER-associated degradation.
source: When a AAA ATPase involved in ER-associated degradation, Cdc48, was recruited to Pex3 through the similar FRB/Rap/FKBP system (cells coexpressing Pex3-FRB and FKBP-Cdc48), Atg36 phosphorylation was not repressed under rapamycin treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Cdc48's function.

claim: Pex15 promotes Pex1/6 association with Pex3 on the surface of peroxisomes but is not strictly required for Atg36 inhibition.
source: Thus, Pex15 promotes Pex1/6 association with Pex3 on the surface of peroxisomes but is not strictly required for Atg36 inhibition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rapamycin-induced tethering experiments that bypass Pex15.

claim: Incubation of Atg36 with wild-type Hrr25 and radiolabeled ATP results in time-dependent appearance of 32P-labeled Atg36 species with progressively reduced gel mobility.
source: Incubation with wild-type but not kinase-dead (K38A) Hrr25 resulted in the time-dependent appearance of 32P-labeled Atg36 species with progressively reduced gel mobility following SDS–PAGE and autoradiography (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Incubation of Atg36 with kinase-dead (K38A) Hrr25 and radiolabeled ATP does not result in appearance of 32P-labeled Atg36 species.
source: Incubation with wild-type but not kinase-dead (K38A) Hrr25 resulted in the time-dependent appearance of 32P-labeled Atg36 species with progressively reduced gel mobility following SDS–PAGE and autoradiography (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The addition of Pex1/6 purified from E. coli inhibits overall Atg36 phosphorylation by ~70% in vitro.
source: Strikingly, the addition of Pex1/6 purified from E. coli (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) inhibited overall Atg36 phosphorylation by ~70%, whereas control incubations with Pex1/6WB were indistinguishable from those lacking Pex1/6 altogether (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Control incubations with Pex1/6WB are indistinguishable from those lacking Pex1/6 altogether in terms of Atg36 phosphorylation.
source: Strikingly, the addition of Pex1/6 purified from E. coli (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) inhibited overall Atg36 phosphorylation by ~70%, whereas control incubations with Pex1/6WB were indistinguishable from those lacking Pex1/6 altogether (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Recombinant Cdc48 has only a marginal, ATPase-dependent effect (~10%) on Atg36 phosphorylation in vitro.
source: First, we replaced Pex1/6 with recombinant Cdc48 (and a control ATPase-defective mutant E558Q, Cdc48D2; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), a homomeric hexamer with a similar AAA+ architecture, and found only a marginal, ATPase-dependent effect on Atg36 phosphorylation (~10%).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Cdc48 is a homomeric hexamer with a similar AAA+ architecture to Pex1/6.
source: First, we replaced Pex1/6 with recombinant Cdc48 (and a control ATPase-defective mutant E558Q, Cdc48D2; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), a homomeric hexamer with a similar AAA+ architecture, and found only a marginal, ATPase-dependent effect on Atg36 phosphorylation (~10%).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Cdc48's structure.

claim: Wild-type preparations of Pex1/6 and Cdc48 have comparable basal ATPase activities.
source: Notably, the wild-type preparations of Pex1/6 and Cdc48 had comparable basal ATPase activities (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Atg19 is a CVT pathway receptor that becomes phosphoactivated by Hrr25 during nutrient starvation.
source: Second, we substituted Atg19 for Atg36 as the substrate because this CVT pathway receptor also becomes phosphoactivated by Hrr25 during nutrient starvation (Pfaffenwimmer et al., 2014; Tanaka et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Pfaffenwimmer et al., 2014; Tanaka et al., 2014).

claim: Pex1/6 does not inhibit Atg19 phosphorylation in the presence or absence of Atg36 in vitro.
source: This control reaction revealed that Pex1/6 did not inhibit Atg19 phosphorylation in the presence or absence of Atg36 (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The Pex1/6 inhibition of phosphorylation is specific to Atg36.
source: Thus, the Pex1/6 inhibition was specific to Atg36.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that Pex1/6 inhibits Atg36 but not Atg19 phosphorylation.

claim: The biochemical data provide complementary support for a model in which the exportomer directly inhibits Atg36 phosphoactivation by Hrr25.
source: Taken together with our previous in vivo evidence, these biochemical data provide complementary support for a model in which the exportomer directly inhibits Atg36 phosphoactivation by Hrr25.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined in vitro and in vivo experimental data.

claim: Atg36 is a novel exportomer substrate.
source: Our in vitro evidence suggests that Atg36 is a novel exportomer substrate.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the in vitro data showing direct interaction and regulation.

claim: Atg36 is predicted to be a largely unstructured protein.
source: Unlike these putative substrates, Atg36 is predicted to be a largely unstructured protein (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by computational predictions shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Atg36 selectively interacts with Pex1 but not Pex6 in a yeast-two-hybrid assay.
source: Thus, we took a yeast-two-hybrid (Y2H) approach and found that Atg36 selectively interacted with Pex1 but not Pex6 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The interaction between Atg36 and Pex1 is fully abolished by N-terminal truncation of the first 30 amino acids of Atg36.
source: This interaction was fully abolished by N-terminal truncation of the first 30 amino acids of Atg36 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The N-terminal 30 amino acids of Atg36 are necessary but not sufficient for Atg36 interaction with Pex1.
source: This region is necessary but not sufficient for Atg36 interaction with Pex1, as a fragment corresponding to the N-terminal 59 amino acids of Atg36, but not a fragment corresponding to the N-terminal 30 amino acids, was able to interact with Pex1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: N-terminal truncations of Atg36 still efficiently localize to peroxisomes.
source: Importantly, cell microscopy analysis revealed that even more severe N-terminal truncations of Atg36 still efficiently localized to peroxisomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A C-terminal sequence determinant for peroxisome localization resides between amino acids 150 and 219 of Atg36.
source: thus pointing us to the existence of a C-terminal sequence determinant for peroxisome localization residing between amino acids 150 and 219 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: Atg36 phosphorylation is enhanced by the ∆N30atg36 mutation.
source: Specifically, Atg36 phosphorylation was enhanced by the ∆N30atg36 mutation, which was also associated with an Atg11-dependent increase in Pex11-GFP processing (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The ∆N30atg36 mutation is associated with an Atg11-dependent increase in Pex11-GFP processing.
source: Specifically, Atg36 phosphorylation was enhanced by the ∆N30atg36 mutation, which was also associated with an Atg11-dependent increase in Pex11-GFP processing (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: More severe N-terminal truncations of Atg36 that are proximal to the Atg11-binding site result in loss of the constitutive pexophagy phenotype.
source: More severe truncations that are proximal to the Atg11-binding site resulted in the loss of this constitutive pexophagy phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Pex15N-∆N30Atg36 binds Pex6 as measured in a Y2H assay.
source: As predicted, Pex15N-∆N30Atg36 bound Pex6 as measured in a Y2H assay (Figure 4B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cells expressing Pex15N-∆N30Atg36 exhibit reduced Atg36 phosphorylation relative to cells expressing ∆N30atg36.
source: and cells expressing Pex15N-∆N30Atg36 exhibited both reduced Atg36 phosphorylation and reduced Pex11-GFP processing (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) relative to cells expressing ∆N30atg36.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Cells expressing Pex15N-∆N30Atg36 exhibit reduced Pex11-GFP processing relative to cells expressing ∆N30atg36.
source: and cells expressing Pex15N-∆N30Atg36 exhibited both reduced Atg36 phosphorylation and reduced Pex11-GFP processing (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) relative to cells expressing ∆N30atg36.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The Y2H interaction between Pex15N-∆N30Atg36 and Pex6 is abolished by introduction of the L22S mutation in Pex15.
source: Importantly, both the Y2H interaction and pexophagy suppression phenotypes were abolished by introduction of a mutation in Pex15 that disrupts the Pex6–Pex15 interaction (L22S) (Birschmann et al., 2003; Figure 4B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, C and citation to prior work (Birschmann et al., 2003).

claim: The pexophagy suppression phenotype of Pex15N-∆N30Atg36 is abolished by introduction of the L22S mutation in Pex15.
source: Importantly, both the Y2H interaction and pexophagy suppression phenotypes were abolished by introduction of a mutation in Pex15 that disrupts the Pex6–Pex15 interaction (L22S) (Birschmann et al., 2003; Figure 4B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, C and citation to prior work (Birschmann et al., 2003).

claim: The L22S mutation in Pex15 disrupts the Pex6–Pex15 interaction.
source: Importantly, both the Y2H interaction and pexophagy suppression phenotypes were abolished by introduction of a mutation in Pex15 that disrupts the Pex6–Pex15 interaction (L22S) (Birschmann et al., 2003; Figure 4B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Birschmann et al., 2003).

claim: The data support a model in which the exportomer directly binds Atg36 to repress Atg36 phosphoactivation by Hrr25.
source: In sum, these data further support a model in which the exportomer directly binds Atg36 to repress Atg36 phosphoactivation by Hrr25.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data with the engineered Pex15N-∆N30Atg36 construct.

claim: Yeast peroxisomes are constitutively degraded by selective autophagy in the absence of exportomer function.
source: Yeast peroxisomes are constitutively degraded by selective autophagy in the absence of exportomer function (Nuttall et al., 2014), but the mechanistic basis for this phenomenon has remained unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Nuttall et al., 2014).

claim: The exportomer prevents pexophagy in unstarved cells by directly repressing phosphoactivation of the yeast pexophagy receptor, Atg36, by the casein kinase Hrr25.
source: In this work, we have presented evidence that the exportomer prevents pexophagy in unstarved cells by directly repressing phosphoactivation of the yeast pexophagy receptor, Atg36, by the casein kinase Hrr25.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ability of the exportomer to repress Atg36 phosphorylation is independent of its known role in membrane extraction of peroxisome proteins.
source: The ability of the exportomer to repress Atg36 phosphorylation is independent of its known role in membrane extraction of peroxisome proteins, as we showed that the exportomer is able to inhibit Atg36 phosphorylation away from the peroxisome or when reconstituted in vitro with purified soluble components.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data with cytosolic constructs and in vitro reconstitution.

claim: Repression of Atg36 phosphorylation by the exportomer requires its AAA-ATPase activity.
source: Repression of Atg36 phosphorylation by the exportomer requires its AAA-ATPase activity, but does not strictly require Pex15, whose function was bypassed by artificial tethering of Pex1/6 to Pex3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data with the Walker B mutant and rapamycin-induced tethering.

claim: Repression of Atg36 phosphorylation by the exportomer does not strictly require Pex15.
source: Repression of Atg36 phosphorylation by the exportomer requires its AAA-ATPase activity, but does not strictly require Pex15, whose function was bypassed by artificial tethering of Pex1/6 to Pex3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data with rapamycin-induced tethering that bypasses Pex15.

claim: Pex1/6 physically interacts with Atg36.
source: We found that Pex1/6 physically interacts with Atg36 and mapped the binding site on Atg36 to its N-terminal region.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Y2H assays and in vitro experiments.

claim: The binding site for Pex1/6 on Atg36 is in its N-terminal region.
source: We found that Pex1/6 physically interacts with Atg36 and mapped the binding site on Atg36 to its N-terminal region.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Y2H assays with truncation mutants.

claim: Deletion of the N-terminal region of Atg36 renders it constitutively active and induces pexophagy.
source: Deletion of this region of Atg36 rendered it constitutively active and induced pexophagy, suggesting that the interaction between Atg36 and Pex1/6 is critical for repression of phosphorylation and pexophagy.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The interaction between Atg36 and Pex1/6 is critical for repression of phosphorylation and pexophagy.
source: Deletion of this region of Atg36 rendered it constitutively active and induced pexophagy, suggesting that the interaction between Atg36 and Pex1/6 is critical for repression of phosphorylation and pexophagy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that deletion of the Pex1-binding region activates Atg36.

claim: Pex3 is required for Atg36 phosphorylation.
source: Pex3 is required for Atg36 phosphorylation, and it was recently shown that Pex3 promotes Atg36 phosphoactivation by enhancing interaction of the Pex3–Atg36 complex with Hrr25 (Meguro et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Meguro et al., 2020).

claim: Pex3 promotes Atg36 phosphoactivation by enhancing interaction of the Pex3–Atg36 complex with Hrr25.
source: Pex3 is required for Atg36 phosphorylation, and it was recently shown that Pex3 promotes Atg36 phosphoactivation by enhancing interaction of the Pex3–Atg36 complex with Hrr25 (Meguro et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Meguro et al., 2020).

claim: Pex3 is not absolutely essential for inhibition of Atg36 phosphorylation by Pex1/6, as Pex1/6 was capable of inhibiting Hrr25-mediated phosphorylation of Atg36 in in vitro assays conducted in the absence of Pex3.
source: It additionally remains unclear whether Pex3 regulates inhibition of Atg36 phosphorylation by Pex1/6, but our work suggests that Pex3 is not absolutely essential for this process, as Pex1/6 was capable of inhibiting Hrr25-mediated phosphorylation of Atg36 in in vitro assays conducted in the absence of Pex3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the in vitro reconstitution experiments that lack Pex3.

claim: Pex3 coimmunoprecipitates with exportomer subunits.
source: While Pex3 coimmunoprecipitates with exportmer subunits in this and previous studies (Weir et al., 2017), we were not able to distinguish whether the coimmunoprecipitation reflected direct interaction between Pex3 and Pex1/6/15 or was mediated by the unidentified factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in this study and citation to prior work (Weir et al., 2017).

claim: An early split-ubiquitin assay study reported a weak interaction signal between Pex15 and Pex3.
source: An early split-ubiquitin assay study reported a weak interaction signal between Pex15 and Pex3 (Eckert and Johnsson, 2003), but no binding between the cytosolic fragments of Pex3 (cytoPex3) and Pex15 (cytoPex15) in our Y2H assay was detected.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Eckert and Johnsson, 2003).

claim: No binding between the cytosolic fragments of Pex3 (cytoPex3) and Pex15 (cytoPex15) was detected in Y2H assay.
source: An early split-ubiquitin assay study reported a weak interaction signal between Pex15 and Pex3 (Eckert and Johnsson, 2003), but no binding between the cytosolic fragments of Pex3 (cytoPex3) and Pex15 (cytoPex15) in our Y2H assay was detected.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Y2H assays.

claim: Atg36 is known to become phosphorylated by Hrr25 upon starvation.
source: Atg36 is known to become phosphorylated by Hrr25 upon starvation, but future studies are required to determine how Atg36 phosphorylation is regulated by changes in nutrient status, and how starvation causes Atg36 to be released from, or overcome, inhibition by Pex1/6.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Atg36 regulation.

claim: Starvation increases Hrr25-mediated phosphorylation of two other autophagy receptors, Atg19 and Atg34.
source: It is known that starvation also increases Hrr25-mediated phosphorylation of two other autophagy receptors, Atg19 and Atg34 (Mochida et al., 2014; Pfaffenwimmer et al., 2014; Tanaka et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mochida et al., 2014; Pfaffenwimmer et al., 2014; Tanaka et al., 2014).

claim: Pex1/6 are mechanonenzymes for both membrane recycling and degradation of Pex5/7, the receptors for targeting soluble proteins to the peroxisome matrix.
source: By analogy, Pex1/6 are known to be mechanonenzymes for both membrane recycling and degradation of Pex5/7, the receptors for targeting soluble proteins to the peroxisome matrix (Hagstrom et al., 2014; Kragt et al., 2005; Miyata and Fujiki, 2005; Platta et al., 2005, Platta et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hagstrom et al., 2014; Kragt et al., 2005; Miyata and Fujiki, 2005; Platta et al., 2005, Platta et al., 2007).

claim: The exportomer also appears to function as a repressor of selective pexophagy in mammalian cells.
source: Finally, even though the exportomer also appears to function as a repressor of selective pexophagy in mammalian cells (Law et al., 2017), it remains unclear whether the mechanism we have uncovered in yeast is relevant to the regulation of pexophagy in mammalian cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Law et al., 2017).

claim: Several important differences exist in the regulation of pexophagy between yeast and mammals, including the use of different autophagy receptor proteins.
source: Several important differences in the regulation of pexophagy between yeast and mammals – including the use of different autophagy receptor proteins and the apparently unique role of ubiquitin in mammalian pexophagy (Deosaran et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2008; Nordgren et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015) – warrant caution in seeking for convergence between these mechanisms.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about differences between yeast and mammalian pexophagy.

claim: Ubiquitin has an apparently unique role in mammalian pexophagy.
source: Several important differences in the regulation of pexophagy between yeast and mammals – including the use of different autophagy receptor proteins and the apparently unique role of ubiquitin in mammalian pexophagy (Deosaran et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2008; Nordgren et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015) – warrant caution in seeking for convergence between these mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Deosaran et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2008; Nordgren et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).

claim: Autophagy receptor proteins facilitate lysosomal destruction of various organelles in response to cellular stress, including nutrient deprivation.
source: Autophagy receptor (or adaptor) proteins facilitate lysosomal destruction of various organelles in response to cellular stress, including nutrient deprivation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about autophagy receptors.

claim: Latent activation of the yeast pexophagy receptor Atg36 by the casein kinase Hrr25 in rich media is repressed by the ATPase activity of Pex1/6.
source: We find that latent activation of the yeast pexophagy receptor Atg36 by the casein kinase Hrr25 in rich media is repressed by the ATPase activity of Pex1/6, the catalytic subunits of the exportomer AAA+ transmembrane complex enabling protein import into peroxisomes.
evidence: The claim is the main finding inferred from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pex1/6 are the catalytic subunits of the exportomer AAA+ transmembrane complex enabling protein import into peroxisomes.
source: We find that latent activation of the yeast pexophagy receptor Atg36 by the casein kinase Hrr25 in rich media is repressed by the ATPase activity of Pex1/6, the catalytic subunits of the exportomer AAA+ transmembrane complex enabling protein import into peroxisomes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Pex1/6 function.

claim: Quantitative proteomics of purified Pex3 support a model in which the exportomer tail anchored to the peroxisome membrane represses Atg36 phosphorylation on Pex3 without assistance from additional membrane factors.
source: Quantitative proteomics of purified Pex3, an obligate Atg36 coreceptor, support a model in which the exportomer tail anchored to the peroxisome membrane represses Atg36 phosphorylation on Pex3 without assistance from additional membrane factors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the quantitative proteomics data.

claim: Pex3 is an obligate Atg36 coreceptor.
source: Quantitative proteomics of purified Pex3, an obligate Atg36 coreceptor, support a model in which the exportomer tail anchored to the peroxisome membrane represses Atg36 phosphorylation on Pex3 without assistance from additional membrane factors.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Pex3's role with Atg36.

claim: Inhibition of Atg36 phosphorylation can be reconstituted in vitro using soluble Pex1/6.
source: Indeed, we reconstitute inhibition of Atg36 phosphorylation in vitro using soluble Pex1/6 and define an N-terminal unstructured region of Atg36 that enables regulation by binding to Pex1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro reconstitution experiments.

claim: An N-terminal unstructured region of Atg36 enables regulation by binding to Pex1.
source: Indeed, we reconstitute inhibition of Atg36 phosphorylation in vitro using soluble Pex1/6 and define an N-terminal unstructured region of Atg36 that enables regulation by binding to Pex1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Y2H assays and in vitro experiments.

claim: A compartment-specific AAA+ complex mediating organelle biogenesis and protein quality control can stave off induction of selective autophagy.
source: Our findings uncover a mechanism by which a compartment-specific AAA+ complex mediating organelle biogenesis and protein quality control staves off induction of selective autophagy.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The accumulation of damaged organelles is a hallmark of aging and neurodegenerative disease.
source: The accumulation of damaged organelles is a hallmark of aging and neurodegenerative disease (Mizushima and Levine, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Mizushima and Levine, 2020).

claim: In healthy cells, damaged organelles are detected and eliminated by selective autophagy.
source: In healthy cells, damaged organelles are detected and eliminated by selective autophagy, a process that involves the capture of organelles in transport vesicles called autophagosomes that deliver organelles to the lysosome for degradation (Gatica et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Gatica et al., 2018).

claim: Selective autophagy involves the capture of organelles in transport vesicles called autophagosomes that deliver organelles to the lysosome for degradation.
source: In healthy cells, damaged organelles are detected and eliminated by selective autophagy, a process that involves the capture of organelles in transport vesicles called autophagosomes that deliver organelles to the lysosome for degradation (Gatica et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Gatica et al., 2018).

claim: Autophagy receptors target a diverse range of organelles and other targets for autophagic degradation.
source: A class of proteins called autophagy receptors targets a diverse range of organelles and other targets for autophagic degradation (Kirkin and Rogov, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Kirkin and Rogov, 2019).

claim: Autophagy receptors function not only by tethering autophagy targets to autophagosomes, but also by initiating de novo autophagosome formation via activation of the master autophagy kinase, Atg1/ULK1.
source: Recent work in yeast and mammals has established that autophagy receptors function not only by tethering autophagy targets to autophagosomes, but also by initiating de novo autophagosome formation via activation of the master autophagy kinase, Atg1/ULK1 (Kamber et al., 2015; Ravenhill et al., 2019; Torggler et al., 2016; Vargas et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kamber et al., 2015; Ravenhill et al., 2019; Torggler et al., 2016; Vargas et al., 2019).

claim: Autophagy receptors must initiate degradation of damaged organelles while sparing functional organelles to perform effective quality control.
source: To perform effective quality control, autophagy receptors must initiate degradation of damaged organelles while sparing functional organelles (Green and Levine, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Green and Levine, 2014).

claim: The localization of multiple autophagy receptors is regulated by organelle damage, such that some receptors localize only to damaged organelles.
source: First, the localization of multiple autophagy receptors is regulated by organelle damage, such that some receptors localize only to damaged organelles (Rogov et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Rogov et al., 2014).

claim: Phosphorylation by cytosolic kinases is critical for the ability of several autophagy receptors to drive organelle degradation.
source: Second, phosphorylation by cytosolic kinases is critical for the ability of several autophagy receptors to drive organelle degradation (Farré et al., 2013; Tanaka et al., 2014; Wild et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Farré et al., 2013; Tanaka et al., 2014; Wild et al., 2011).

claim: The kinase TBK1 is recruited to depolarized mitochondria, where it phosphoactivates the autophagy receptor OPTN, enabling selective elimination of damaged mitochondria.
source: Studies of mitochondrial autophagy in mammalian cells have shown that such receptor phosphorylation events can be regulated to enable effective organelle quality control: the kinase TBK1 is recruited to depolarized mitochondria, where it phosphoactivates the autophagy receptor OPTN, enabling selective elimination of damaged mitochondria (Moore and Holzbaur, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Moore and Holzbaur, 2016).

claim: Peroxisomes are rapidly degraded by autophagy in cells that lack Pex1, Pex6, or Pex15.
source: Recently, multiple groups working in yeast and mammalian cells reported intriguing observations that peroxisomes are rapidly degraded by autophagy in cells that lack Pex1, Pex6, or Pex15 (Law et al., 2017; Nuttall et al., 2014), which form a complex required for peroxisome matrix protein import (Platta et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Law et al., 2017; Nuttall et al., 2014).

claim: Pex1, Pex6, and Pex15 form a complex required for peroxisome matrix protein import.
source: Recently, multiple groups working in yeast and mammalian cells reported intriguing observations that peroxisomes are rapidly degraded by autophagy in cells that lack Pex1, Pex6, or Pex15 (Law et al., 2017; Nuttall et al., 2014), which form a complex required for peroxisome matrix protein import (Platta et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Platta et al., 2013).

claim: The Pex1/6 subunits form a hexameric AAA-ATPase that is recruited by Pex15 to peroxisomes.
source: The Pex1/6 subunits form a hexameric AAA-ATPase that is recruited by Pex15 to peroxisomes, where it extracts ubiquitinated Pex5 (a receptor for peroxisome matrix proteins) from the peroxisome membrane to enable additional rounds of protein import (Platta et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Platta et al., 2005).

claim: The Pex1/6 hexameric AAA-ATPase extracts ubiquitinated Pex5 from the peroxisome membrane to enable additional rounds of protein import.
source: The Pex1/6 subunits form a hexameric AAA-ATPase that is recruited by Pex15 to peroxisomes, where it extracts ubiquitinated Pex5 (a receptor for peroxisome matrix proteins) from the peroxisome membrane to enable additional rounds of protein import (Platta et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Platta et al., 2005).

claim: Pex5 is a receptor for peroxisome matrix proteins.
source: The Pex1/6 subunits form a hexameric AAA-ATPase that is recruited by Pex15 to peroxisomes, where it extracts ubiquitinated Pex5 (a receptor for peroxisome matrix proteins) from the peroxisome membrane to enable additional rounds of protein import (Platta et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Pex5's function.

claim: The accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins on the surface of peroxisomes drives selective peroxisome autophagy in mammalian cells.
source: The accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins on the surface of peroxisomes has been shown to drive selective peroxisome autophagy (also known as pexophagy) in mammalian cells (Deosaran et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Deosaran et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2008).

claim: It was proposed that the accumulation of ubiquitinated Pex5 in exportomer-deficient cells explains why pexophagy is induced in those cells.
source: and it was thus proposed that the accumulation of ubiquitinated Pex5 in exportomer-deficient cells explains why pexophagy is induced in those cells (Law et al., 2017; Nazarko, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Law et al., 2017; Nazarko, 2017).

claim: Pex5 is not required for pexophagy in exportomer-deficient yeast cells.
source: However, it remains to be determined why pexophagy is induced by exportomer mutations in yeast, as Pex5 is not required for pexophagy in exportomer-deficient cells and ubiquitination does not appear to be a pexophagy-inducing signal in yeast (Nuttall et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Nuttall et al., 2014).

claim: Ubiquitination does not appear to be a pexophagy-inducing signal in yeast.
source: However, it remains to be determined why pexophagy is induced by exportomer mutations in yeast, as Pex5 is not required for pexophagy in exportomer-deficient cells and ubiquitination does not appear to be a pexophagy-inducing signal in yeast (Nuttall et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Nuttall et al., 2014).

claim: All forms of budding yeast pexophagy, including pexophagy driven by exportomer loss, are dependent on the autophagy receptor Atg36.
source: All forms of budding yeast pexophagy, including pexophagy driven by exportomer loss, are dependent on the autophagy receptor Atg36 (Motley et al., 2012; Nuttall et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Motley et al., 2012; Nuttall et al., 2014).

claim: The ability of Atg36 to drive pexophagy depends on its phosphoactivation.
source: whose ability to drive pexophagy depends on its phosphoactivation (Farré et al., 2013; Tanaka et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Farré et al., 2013; Tanaka et al., 2014).
